claims.text: Increasing Cr concentration in a high-entropy-alloy coating promotes stress-induced formation of a spinel oxide tribolayer during sliding wear.
The Cr-promoted spinel tribolayer reduces wear rate relative to a lower-Cr coating.
An alloy analogous to AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 has a multiphase microstructure.
The cited AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 material is representative of a deposited protective coating.
Cr concentration can be increased during coating deposition, for example by sputter deposition.
Increasing Cr concentration directly enhances the alloy's oxophilicity.
Atmospheric oxygen assists oxide formation during sliding wear.
Sliding wear produces a protective oxide tribolayer in AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 under elevated-temperature atmospheric conditions.
The protective tribolayer is specifically a stress-induced spinel oxide.
Additional Cr causes a rapidly forming, more continuous, and more robust oxide layer during wear.
The oxide tribolayer acts as a diffusion barrier and load distributor.
A protective oxide layer can reduce mechanical wear in AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 at elevated temperature.
The elevated-Cr coating will have a lower wear rate than the baseline coating.
The elevated-Cr coating will have a lower coefficient of friction than the baseline coating.
The elevated-Cr coating will form a thicker or more continuous spinel oxide tribolayer than the baseline.
The baseline coating forms only a patchy or less effective tribolayer during sliding wear.
The proposed effect should hold from room temperature to moderately elevated temperature when sufficient oxygen is available.
Very high temperatures or severely reducing atmospheres may not show the proposed Cr-wear trend.
Other elements such as Mn can dominate oxide formation in some high-entropy alloys, complicating attribution to Cr.
Failure to obtain either a statistically significant wear/friction reduction or an enhanced protective spinel tribolayer in the high-Cr coating would falsify the proposed mechanism.
